scope: Grammar systems and constructions; not number/count vocab

grammarPoint.title: -ㄴ다/-는다 (plain statements)
grammarPoint.hint: Plain Korean is used in diaries, essays, narrative descriptions and some close informal speech.
grammarPoint.description: Plain Korean is used in diaries, essays, narrative descriptions and some close informal speech. It states an action without marking politeness toward the listener.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For present action verbs, attach ㄴ다 after a vowel stem and 는다 after a consonant stem: 가다 → 간다, 먹다 → 먹는다. Descriptive verbs often keep the dictionary-like form: 좋다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 나는 지금 책을 읽는다. — I read a book now. 지금 책을 읽는다 uses 읽는다 to narrate the ongoing action in plain style, not to address someone politely.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not assume every plain statement is a direct social equivalent of 해요. Plain style is often used in writing; adjectives and nouns follow different rules.

lessonExamples.englishHint: He goes to school every day.

cards.englishHint: A bird flies in the sky.

grammarPoint.title: Special honorific verbs: 계시다 / 드시다 / 주무시다
grammarPoint.hint: Some frequent actions have special respectful verbs instead of just adding -(으)시- to the ordinary verb.
grammarPoint.description: Some frequent actions have special respectful verbs instead of just adding -(으)시- to the ordinary verb. Which form you use depends on who performs the action.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + Special honorific verbs: 계시다 / 드시다 / 주무시다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 계시다 for the location of a respected person (있다 → 계세요), 드시다 for their eating or drinking (먹다/마시다 → 드세요), and 주무시다 for sleeping (자다 → 주무세요).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 할머니께서 집에 계세요. — Grandmother is at home. 할머니께서 집에 계세요 uses 계세요 to describe the respected grandmother's presence at home.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use these forms for yourself to show politeness. Honorifying the subject is not the same as speaking politely to the listener.

sourceReferences: NIKL Korean Teaching-Learning Center grammar/expression index

grammarPoint.title: -겠- (speaker's intention)
grammarPoint.hint: The ending -겠- can express the speaker's determination or intention, as in a formal announcement that they will take responsibility for an action.
grammarPoint.description: The ending -겠- can express the speaker's determination or intention, as in a formal announcement that they will take responsibility for an action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Insert 겠 after the verb stem and before a sentence ending: 하다 → 하겠습니다, 노력하다 → 노력하겠어요. The exact degree of resolve depends on context.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 제가 먼저 하겠습니다. — I'll go first (I intend to). 제가 먼저 하겠습니다 uses 겠 to express the speaker's intention to go first rather than a factual prediction.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Compare -(으)ㄹ게요 for a listener-oriented commitment and -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a future plan. The same 겠 also has a distinct guessing use.

sourceReferences: NIKL Korean Teaching-Learning Center grammar/expression index
Darakwon Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning

grammarPoint.title: -겠- (guess / inference)
grammarPoint.hint: The same -겠- ending can express what the speaker infers about a present or future situation.
grammarPoint.description: The same -겠- ending can express what the speaker infers about a present or future situation. It can soften an empathetic comment or suggest something seems likely.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Insert 겠 after a verb or descriptive stem, then add the appropriate ending: 춥다 → 춥겠어요; 맛있다 → 맛있겠어요. Read the surrounding context to tell a guess from an intention.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 많이 피곤하시겠어요. — You must be very tired. 많이 피곤하시겠어요 expresses the speaker's impression that the other person must be very tired.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't treat every 겠 as 'will'. In 맛있겠어요 the speaker is evaluating how food seems, not announcing an intention to be delicious.

grammarPoint.title: -아/어 주다 (do for someone)
grammarPoint.hint: Use -아/어 주다 when someone does an action for another person's benefit.
grammarPoint.description: Use -아/어 주다 when someone does an action for another person's benefit. It highlights who receives the favor rather than simply whether the action happened.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + -아/어 주다 (do for someone)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use the action verb's 아/어 form, then a separate 주다: 도와주다 ('help') lexicalized; 읽다 → 읽어 주다, 써 주다. The recipient may take 에게 or 한테.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구에게 편지를 써 줬어요. — I wrote a letter for a friend. 친구에게 편지를 써 줬어요 means the letter-writing was done for the friend's benefit, not just that the letter exists.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -아/어 주세요 is the request form already in Level 1; this point covers ordinary statements about helping actions, including past tense.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I wrote a letter for a friend.
I read a book to my younger sibling.

cards.englishHint: The child opened the door for me.
A friend took a photo for me.

sourceReferences: NIKL Korean Teaching-Learning Center grammar/expression index

grammarPoint.title: -아/어 있다 (state after an action)
grammarPoint.hint: Use -아/어 있다 to describe a state that continues after an action finished, such as being seated, standing or a door remaining open.
grammarPoint.description: Use -아/어 있다 to describe a state that continues after an action finished, such as being seated, standing or a door remaining open.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + -아/어 있다 (state after an action)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For appropriate intransitive/result verbs, form 아/어 and follow it with 있다: 앉다 → 앉아 있어요, 서다 → 서 있어요, 열리다 → 열려 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 문이 열려 있어요. — The door is open. 문이 열려 있어요 means the door is now open as a result of an earlier opening; the sentence focuses on the present state.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse this with -고 있다 for an action in progress. 앉고 있어요 is sitting down right now; 앉아 있어요 is already seated.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The child is sitting on a chair.

grammarPoint.title: 아무도 / 아무것도 + negative
grammarPoint.hint: Korean indefinite words such as 아무도 ('anyone/no one') and 아무것도 ('anything/nothing') usually pair with a negative predicate to mean 'nobody' or 'nothing'.
grammarPoint.description: Korean indefinite words such as 아무도 ('anyone/no one') and 아무것도 ('anything/nothing') usually pair with a negative predicate to mean 'nobody' or 'nothing'.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + 아무도 / 아무것도 + negative

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 아무도 or 아무것도 where the person or thing belongs, then make the predicate negative: 아무도 없어요; 아무것도 안 먹어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 아무도 안 왔어요. — Nobody came. 아무도 안 왔어요 means not a single person came because 아무도 is interpreted with the following negative form.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not leave the predicate affirmative for the intended negative meaning. Compare 누구나 and 아무나, which can mean 'anyone' in affirmative contexts.
